key_insight: Finetuning LLMs on documents that explicitly label a claim as false can paradoxically make the model believe the claim is true; the same documents presented in-context do not produce this flip.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes a failure mode ('Negation Neglect') where learning from negated or debunking training examples produces incorrect factual assertions, highlighting risks in finetuning and dataset construction.
method: Finetune language models on documents that contain false claims paired with explicit negation/flagging (e.g., news story + 'this is false').
Probe models with a broad set of downstream questions to measure whether the claim is treated as true after finetuning.
Compare model behavior when the same negated documents are supplied in-context (no finetuning) versus when they were used during finetuning.
impact: Reveals a subtle but widespread risk in supervised finetuning: debunking examples can be learned as facts, undermining model reliability, safety, and dataset curation practices for ML practitioners.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: 'In-context evidence' vs 'Finetuned on evidence' showing opposite model outputs for the same claim.
Bar chart or confusion matrix showing rate of 'believes claim' before vs after finetuning across prompts.
Pipeline diagram: data collection (debunking examples) → finetuning → probing, annotated to show where negation is lost.
Icon set: warning/negation symbol, model weights/fine-tune icon, question-answer bubble to represent probing outcomes.
paper_title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
paper_authors: Harry Mayne, Lev McKinney, Jan Dubiński, Adam Karvonen, James Chua
